newsitem.title: FRANCE: Major trumpets Britain's economic lead over France.
newsitem.headline: Major trumpets Britain's economic lead over France.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major gave France an economics lesson before a summit with President Jacques Chirac on Thursday, saying Britain had a far better record of creating jobs and avoiding strikes.

Major was to meet Chirac over dinner in the south-western wine capital of Bordeaux, starting a two-day summit at which France will press Britain to join a planned multinational force to protect refugees in Zaire.

Major, trailing the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls ahead of elections due by May 1997, gave a rosy picture of the British economy and contrasted it with France, where unemployment is at record highs.

He said that average families in Britain would be 700 sterling ($1,150) better off than at the last election in 1992. "That's why the pulse of Britain is growing stronger. Compare that with what is happening in the rest of Europe."

"Youth unemployment in Britain is 15 percent -- still too high -- but in France it's well over 26 percent," he said in remarks to a British newspaper hours before landing in Bordeaux in the early evening.
"In Britain, we've seen the number of days lost to strikes fall to the lowest ever...In France, many of their public services have been paralysed by walkouts," he said.
Major was more diplomatic in an article in the French daily Le Monde in which he outlined his vision of Europe and cautioned against a headlong rush to European integration.

"I am a European convinced, like the great majority of my compatriots, that the place of Britain is in Europe," Major wrote ahead of the summit, being held amid tight security in Bordeaux after a bomb attack by Corsican guerrillas last month.

He said European nations should be sure that all aspects of Economic and Monetary Union had been examined before pushing ahead with a single European currency from 1999. He said there would be "devastating fallout" if EMU were set up and failed.

Britain remains wary of French and Spanish proposals to send a multinational force of about 5,000 troops to help relief supplies reach more than a million refugees threatened by fighting in eastern Zaire.
British officials say they will listen to French proposals while stressing the problems of such types of action.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, due to discuss the issue with British counterpart Malcolm Rifkind on Friday, lashed out at unnamed reluctant allies on Wednesday, saying: "The main obstacle is the international community's spinelessness."

The idea of setting up a force has gained ground since it was accepted by Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko. Tutsi rebels who have overwhelmed the Zaire army in two eastern provinces say they would oppose French participation.

Chirac and Major, at their last bilateral summit before British elections due by May 1997, will also seek to smooth out differences on EU majority voting and French and German plans for flexibility to let some states integrate faster than others.

The only concrete accord expected is a bilateral agreement to increase naval cooperation, which Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said was part of a drive towards a common European defence policy.
The two countries will sign a letter of intent to increase naval cooperation on issues ranging from arms procurement to training and computers.
